And it must be considered that it is not the ox that is turned to fury, but the lion that is changed to gentleness. The serpent too, which watched for the heel of man, and whose head was watched for by man, will by no means be nourished by the destruction of others, but will eat earth, or dust, as bread (Gen 3). Or certainly it is to be understood thus: that the devil, who formerly fed on the deaths of men, eats only those who are dust and earth: by all of which is shown the change of the wicked into good, who will be harmless, having laid aside their ancient ferocity: not outside, but in the holy mountain of the Lord, that is, in the Church, and in the confession of that mountain by which the prince of Tyre was wounded, and which, cut out of the mountain without hands, grew into a great mountain and filled the world (Dan 2). Let us in this place ask the Jews, and all who under the Christian name still eat the straw of the Scriptures, which, separated from the wheat by the winnowing fan of the Lord, will be given over to the wind and the flames, what blessedness is to be reckoned in this: that in a kingdom of a thousand years, on Mount Zion, in Jerusalem, the city of Christ then present, and in a most august Temple, wolves and lambs, lions and oxen, serpents and men should eat together and dwell alike? and that they should be harmless only to those who have dwelt in the holy mountain of the Lord? From which we understand that all who are outside the mountain are to be slain. So the whole world will be stripped of wolves, lions, bears, leopards and serpents and the other beasts; and the immense woodlands, and the vast waste of the Egyptian desert, which is fertile in venomous creatures; and, as the height of happiness, the holy city will be the dwelling place not only of men but of beasts and serpents, so that, according to the earlier prophecy, the wolf dwells with the lamb, and the leopard with the kid, the calf and the lion, and sheep stay together with bears (Isa 11); and a little child leads them, and an infant from the breast puts his hand into the hole of the asp, and kills the basilisk in its den. And the cause of so great a happiness is that the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord.
Fifth, as to the tranquility of peace: the wolf and the lamb, for those who formerly were tyrants and evildoers will abide peacefully with others, above (Isa 11:6) has the same.
66: Our fathers had the tabernacle of witness in the wilderness, as he had appointed, speaking unto Moses, that he should make it according to the fashion that he had seen.  Which also our fathers that came after brought in with Jesus into the possession of the Gentiles, whom God drave out before the face of our fathers, unto the days of David;  Who found favour before God, and desired to find a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.  But Solomon built him an house.  Howbeit the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands; as saith the prophet,  Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool: what house will ye build me? saith the Lord: or what is the place of my rest?  Hath not my hand made all these things? [Isaiah 66:1-2]
He has not even built a house for himself! He has nothing to do with space. Even if it is written that "the heaven is his throne," he is not contained as the words suggest.

And He has added hereto by the prophet, "The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: what house will ye build me, and where is the place of my rest?" that He may show that He whom the world does not contain is much less contained in a temple; and He says these things not for boastfulness of Himself, but for our knowledge. For He does not desire from us the glory of His magnitude; but He wishes to confer upon us, even as a father, a religious wisdom.

And although the heavenly Scripture often turns the divine appearance into a human form,—as when it says, "The eyes of the Lord are over the righteous;" or when it says, "The Lord God smelled the smell of a good savour;" or when there are given to Moses the tables "written with the finger of God;" or when the people of the children of Israel are set free from the land of Egypt "with a mighty hand and with a stretched out arm;" or when it says, "The mouth of the Lord hath spoken these things;" or when the earth is set forth as "God's footstool;" or when it says, "Incline thine ear, and hear,"—we who say that the law is spiritual do not include within these lineaments of our bodily nature any mode or figure of the divine majesty, but diffuse that character of unbounded magnitude (so to speak) over its plains without any limit. For it is written, "If I shall ascend into heaven, Thou art there; if I shall descend into hell, Thou art there also; and if I shall take my wings, and go away across the sea, there Thy hand shall lay hold of me, and Thy right hand shall hold me." For we recognise the plan of the divine Scripture according to the proportion of its arrangement. For the prophet then was still speaking about God in parables according to the period of the faith, not as God was, but as the people were able to receive Him. And thus, that such things as these should be said about God, must be imputed not to God, but rather to the people. Thus the people are permitted to erect a tabernacle, and yet God is not contained within the enclosure of a tabernacle. Thus a temple is reared, and yet God is not at all bounded within the restraints of a temple. It is not therefore God who is limited, but the perception of the people is limited; nor is God straitened, but the understanding of the reason of the people is held to be straitened. Finally, in the Gospel the Lord said, "The hour shall come when neither in this mountain nor in Jerusalem shall ye worship the Father;" and gave the reasons, saying, "God is a Spirit; and those therefore who worship, must worship in spirit and in truth." Thus the divine agencies are there exhibited by means of members; it is not the appearance of God nor the bodily lineaments that are described. For when the eyes are spoken of, it is implied that He sees all things; and when the ear, it is set forth that He hears all things; and when the finger, a certain energy of His will is opened up; and when the nostrils, His recognition of prayers is shown forth as of odours; and when the hand, it is proved that He is the author of every creature; and when the arm, it is announced that no nature can withstand the power of His arm; and when the feet it is unfolded that He fills all things, and that there is not any place where God is not. For neither members nor the offices of members are needful to Him to whose sole judgment, even unexpressed, all things serve and are present. For why should He require eyes who is Himself the light? or why should He ask for feet who is everywhere? or why should He wish to go when there is nowhere where He can go beyond Himself? or why should He seek for hands whose will is, even when silent, the architect for the foundation of all things? He needs no ears who knows the wills that are even unexpressed; or for what reason should He need a tongue whose thought is a command? These members assuredly were necessary to men, but not to God, because man's design would be ineffectual if the body did not fulfil the thought. Moreover, they are not needful to God, whose will the works attend not so much without any effort, as that the works themselves proceed simultaneously with the will. Moreover, He Himself is all eye, because He all sees; and all ear, because He all hears; and all hand, because He all works; and all foot, because He all is everywhere. For He is the same, whatever it is. He is all equal, and all everywhere. For He has not in Him any diversity in Himself, being simple. For those are the things which are reduced to diversity of members, which arise from birth and go to dissolution. But things which are not concrete cannot be conscious of these things. And what is immortal, whatever it is, that very thing is one and simple, and for ever. And thus because it is one it cannot be dissolved; since whatever is that very thing which is placed beyond the claim of dissolution, it is freed from the laws of death.

Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my seat, and earth the footstool of my feet. What is this house that you will build for me, and what is this place of my rest? All these things my hand has made, and all these things have come to be, says the Lord. LXX likewise. Lest we should understand the holy mountain as Zion and be covered with the Jewish error, who think that Jerusalem is to be built up and that all the things the Lord promises are to be fulfilled there carnally, he takes this suspicion away from us, and sets down the testimony which Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, used against the contentiousness of the Jews (Acts 7). Solomon built him a house, without doubt for God; but the Most High does not dwell in things made with hands, as the Prophet says: Heaven is my throne: but earth is the footstool of my feet. And Paul in the same volume: God, who made the world and those who are in it, by no means dwells in temples made with hands (Acts 17:24). For if, like one sitting on a throne and reigning, heaven is his throne and earth the footstool of his feet, how shall he be shut up in a small place who fills all things, and in whom all things are? Hence Moses too: Do not say, he says, in your heart, He is far off: for God is in heaven above and upon the earth beneath: and there is no other God besides him (Deut 4:39). And the Psalmist: Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I go up into heaven, you are there: if I go down to hell, you are present (Ps 138 [139]:7). With him Jeremiah too agrees, speaking in the person of God: I am a God at hand, and not a God from afar. Can anyone hide in secret places, and I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth (Jer 23:23, 24)? For in him we all are and move (Acts 17). And he says this to refute the Jewish error, who think that the invisible, incorporeal and incomprehensible God can be shut up in the temple of Jerusalem. This indeed Solomon himself, the builder of the Temple, confesses at length in his prayer to the Lord (1 Kgs 8). And lest we think that the greatness of God is to be measured even by heaven and earth, we read of him in another place: Who holds heaven in his palm, and the earth in his fist (Isa 40:12). By these things God is shown to be both outside and within, both poured into and poured around, since he is not shut in by the throne that surrounds him, and he shuts in with his fist and his palm. He is the creator not only of heaven and earth, but also of the invisible Angels and Archangels, Dominions, Powers, and of all men, of whom the Apostle speaks (Col 1): all of which the hand of God has worked. Of this hand both Job and the Psalmist make mention: Your hand has made me and fashioned me (Job 10:18; Ps 118 [119]:73). For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. Of whom John says again: He was in the world, he says, and the world was made through him (John 1). For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps 32 [33]). And this is what the Scripture of Genesis shows in mystical speech: God said, and God made (Gen 1). For by the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth. And there is no place of the Lord's rest except the one which the Prophet adds next.

The Lord is in his holy temple, the Lord's seat is in heaven. Before the bodily temple was built by Solomon, the prophet knows the spiritual temple of the Lord and his throne in heaven. Whereupon it is asked, how it is said elsewhere, "Heaven is my throne." When the throne of the Lord is in heaven, his throne is encompassed by heaven, and the throne of the Lord is in a part of heaven; when heaven is the throne of the Lord, the whole heaven is turned into the throne of the Lord. From which, according to the ἀναγωγήν (higher spiritual sense, anagōgē), the Lord dwelling in his holy temple — that is, in the soul of the believer — dwells either in a part of it or in the whole. When we are still imperfect, and there is in us both something good and something evil, God dwells only in a part of our soul, that is, in heaven. But when we are consummate and perfect, we are wholly turned into a dwelling-place of God, and we are made heaven, his throne.

"Heaven is my throne, while the earth is my footstool." … Haven't you also read that other text, "Who measured the heaven with the palm of his hand?" … Whoever sat in the palm of his own hand?…Does the same heaven become wide when he is sitting in it and narrow when he is measuring it? Or is God the same size in his seat as he is in his palm? If that is the case, God did not make us in his own likeness, because we have palms that are much narrower than the part of the body we sit with. But if he is as broad in the palm as he is broad in the beam, then he made very unequal parts for us. No, that is not where the likeness lies. Such an idol should be ashamed of itself in a Christian mind.
So then, take "heaven" as standing for all the saints, since earth too stands for all who are on the earth, "Let all the earth worship you."

Thou art become a heaven, and fearest thou the earth? For the Scripture saith in another passage, that the Lord our God doth declare, “The heaven is My throne.” If therefore even thou by having the fulness of knowledge, and by having love, hast been made the throne of God, thou hast become a heaven. For this heaven which we look up to with these eyes of ours, is not very precious before God. Holy souls are the heaven of God; the minds of the Angels, and all the minds of His servants, are the heaven of God.

But consider, brethren, what he commandeth us to fall down before. In another passage of the Scriptures it is said, “The heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool.” Doth he then bid us worship the earth, since in another passage it is said, that it is God’s footstool? How then shall we worship the earth, when the Scripture saith openly, “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God”? Yet here it saith, “fall down before His footstool:” and, explaining to us what His footstool is, it saith, “The earth is My footstool.” I am in doubt; I fear to worship the earth, lest He who made the heaven and the earth condemn me; again, I fear not to worship the footstool of my Lord, because the Psalm biddeth me, “fall down before His footstool.” I ask, what is His footstool? and the Scripture telleth me, “the earth is My footstool.” In hesitation I turn unto Christ, since I am herein seeking Himself: and I discover how the earth may be worshipped without impiety, how His footstool may be worshipped without impiety. For He took upon Him earth from earth; because flesh is from earth, and He received flesh from the flesh of Mary. And because He walked here in very flesh, and gave that very flesh to us to eat for our salvation; and no one eateth that flesh, unless he hath first worshipped: we have found out in what sense such a footstool of our Lord’s may be worshipped, and not only that we sin not in worshipping it, but that we sin in not worshipping.

God, then, being immaterial and uncircumscribed, has not place. For He is His own place, filling all things and being above all things, and Himself maintaining all things. Yet we speak of God having place and the place of God where His energy becomes manifest. For He penetrates everything without mixing with it, and imparts to all His energy in proportion to the fitness and receptive power of each: and by this I mean, a purity both natural and voluntary. For the immaterial is purer than the material, and that which is virtuous than that which is linked with vice. Wherefore by the place of God is meant that which has a greater share in His energy and grace. For this reason the Heaven is His throne. For in it are the angels who do His will and are always glorifying Him. For this is His rest and the earth is His footstool. For in it He dwelt in the flesh among men. And His sacred flesh has been named the foot of God. The Church, too, is spoken of as the place of God: for we have set this apart for the glorifying of God as a sort of consecrated place wherein we also hold converse with Him. Likewise also the places in which His energy becomes manifest to us, whether through the flesh or apart from flesh, are spoken of as the places of God.
An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 1, Chapter 13

Thus says the Lord. Here he determines the manner of execution of the sentence. And first, in particular, as to the Jews; second, universally, as to all: but I know their works, and their thoughts (Isa 66:18). The first is divided into two parts: in the first, he excludes false confidence; second, he sets out and determines the sentence that has been given as to the manner of execution: hear the word of the Lord (Isa 66:5).

Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he excludes false trust in the sanctity of the temple, showing that the temple is not the location of God: both from the greatness of God, who fills all things, whose throne is said to be heaven, because it participates greatly in his goodness, as a seat holds the greater part of the one seated; the earth my footstool, because the earth participates least in his goodness, as the outer part of the seated person reaches to the footstool; or, by heaven, he indicates the saints, by earth, the earthly: if heaven, and the heavens of heavens, cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built? (1 Kgs 8:27); do not I fill heaven and earth? (Jer 23:24); God dwells not in temples made with hands (Acts 17:24). And from his rest, for each thing rests in the place which is its own; however, God does not rest in anything, but all things rest in him, as they are made by him: and what is this place of my rest, above: lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these things (Isa 40:26).

Let us therefore, brethren, be of humble mind, laying aside all haughtiness, and pride, and foolishness, and angry feelings; and let us act according to that which is written (for the Holy Spirit saith, "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, neither let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him that glorieth glory in the Lord, in diligently seeking Him, and doing judgment and righteousness" [Jeremiah 9:23-24]), being especially mindful of the words of the Lord Jesus which He spake, teaching us meekness and long-suffering. For thus He spoke: "Be ye merciful, that ye may obtain mercy; forgive, that it may be forgiven to you; as ye do, so shall it be done unto you; as ye judge, so shall ye be judged; as ye are kind, so shall kindness be shown to you; with what measure ye mete, with the same it shall be measured to you." [Matthew 5:7, Matthew 6:14, Matthew 7:1-2] By this precept and by these rules let us establish ourselves, that we walk with all humility in obedience to His holy words. For the holy word saith, "On whom shall I look, but on him that is meek and peaceable, and that trembleth at My words?" [Isaiah 66:2]
Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 13

But you also, who desire to receive the sacred baptism and to merit the grace of the Spirit, ought first to be purged by the law, ought first, having heard the word of God, to cut away your inborn vices and to compose your barbarous and savage ways, so that, having taken up gentleness and humility, you may be able also to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. For thus says the Lord through the prophet: "Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?" If you are not "humble and quiet", the grace of the Holy Spirit cannot dwell in you, if you have not received the divine words with trembling. For the Holy Spirit flees from a proud and stubborn and feigning soul. You ought, therefore, first to meditate on the law of God, so that, if perchance your acts are unrestrained and your ways disordered, the law of God may amend and correct you.

We must preserve in the straight and narrow road of praise and glory; and since peacefulness and humility and the tranquility of a good life are fitting for all Christians, according to the word of the Lord, who looks to no other person than "to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and that trembles at" his word, it the more behooves you confessors, who have been made an example to the rest of the brothers, to observe and fulfill this, as being those whose characters should provoke to imitation the life and conduct of all.

And He, wishing moreover to attract to gentleness our minds, brutish, and swelling, and stubborn with cloddish ferocity, says, "And upon whom shall my Spirit rest, save upon him that is lowly, and quiet, and that trembleth at my words?"—so that in some degree one may recognise how great God is, in learning to fear Him by the Spirit given to him:

Thus also Satan, he has not the knowledge beforehand to know or see when the Spirit will depart, that so he may come to rob the man; but he too listens and watches, and so assails. But if he hears a man in whom Christ dwells speaking shameful words, or enraged, or quarrelling, or contending, then Satan knows that Christ is not with him, and he comes and accomplishes his will in him. For Christ dwells in the peaceful and the meek, and lodges in those that fear His word, as He says through the prophet:—On whom shall I look, and in whom shall I dwell, but in the peaceful and the meek who fear My word? And our Lord said:—Whoever walks in My commandments and keeps My love, We will come to him and make Our abode with him. But if he hears from a man that he is on his guard and is praying and meditating in the Law of his Lord by day and by night, then he turns back from him, for he knows that Christ is with him.

For the prophet says in the person of the Father, "My Hand made all these things," meaning by "Hand," in his dark saying, the power of the Only-begotten. Now the Apostle says that all things are of the Father, and that all things are by the Son, and the prophetic spirit in a way agrees with the Apostolic teaching, which itself also is given through the Spirit. For in the one passage, the prophet, when he says that all things are the work of the Hand of Him Who is over all, sets forth the nature of those things which have come into being in its relation to Him Who made them, while He Who made them is God over all, Who has the Hand, and by It makes all things. And again, in the other passage, the Apostle makes the same division of entities, making all things depend upon their productive cause, yet not reckoning in the number of "all things" that which produces them: so that we are hereby taught the difference of nature between the created and the uncreated, and it is shown that, in its own nature, that which makes is one thing and that which is produced is another.

But to whom shall I look, except to the poor little one and the contrite of spirit, and the one who trembles at my words? He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man. He who slaughters a sheep is as one who brains a dog. He who offers an oblation is as one who offers swine's blood. He who remembers frankincense is as one who blesses an idol. LXX: And upon whom shall I look, except the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words? ÷ But the wicked man ⁚ who sacrifices a calf is as one who strikes down a man. He who sacrifices from the flock is as one who kills a dog. He who offers fine flour is as one who offers swine's blood. He who gives frankincense for a memorial is as a blasphemer. Once the altar and the earthly Temple, which the hand of man had built, have been taken away, the victims of the Jews too are rightly taken away, lest perhaps they should say: We are not so foolish as to think that God can be shut up in a place; but in a place set apart for sacrificing, we sacrifice to God the victims which are prescribed by the law. The inhabitant of heaven, then, or rather the Creator of all, who denies that he has a temple on earth, gladly takes up as his temple the man who is humble and quiet and trembles at his words, according to that saying of the Apostle: But you are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you. If anyone violates the temple of God, God will violate him. For the temple of God is holy, which you are (1 Cor 3:16, 17). Whoever, then, is humble and quiet and trembles at the words of God, him the Lord looks upon; and of him may be understood what is prophesied under the name of the earth: The earth trembled and was quiet, when God arose to judgment (Ps 75 [76]:9, 10). For its inhabitants, for whom the earth is named μετωνυμικῶς, considering the judgment of God, keep quiet from evil works; and sitting at home, rest in an eternal sabbath, so as not to stir themselves to the servile work of sin, as the builders of the tower once moved their feet from the East and left the rising of the true light. Nor did they hear what is said to Cain: You have sinned, be quiet (Gen 4). But according to the Proverbs of Solomon: He who hears God shall dwell confidently, and shall rest without fear from every evil (Prov 1:33). This is the humble and poor little one, contrite of spirit and trembling at the words of the Lord, of whom it is written in the Gospel: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt 5:3). And elsewhere: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor (Ps 40 [41]:1). And again: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor (Isa 61:1).

"On whom does my Spirit rest, if not on one who is humble and quiet and who trembles at my words?" So when he becomes the occupant, he fills and guides and leads the person, restrains from evil and spurs on to good, makes justice delightful, so that the person does good out of love for what is right, not out of fear of punishment. No one is capable on their own of doing what I have said. But if you have the Holy Spirit as the occupant of your house, you will find him also assisting you in everything good.

At these words Peter trembled, Plato did not; so let the fisherman keep what the great and famous philosopher ignored! "You have hidden these things from the wise and the knowing and have revealed them to the little ones."

Where did he seek a place for the Lord? If he was meek, he sought it in himself. For how is one a place for the Lord? Hear the Prophet: “Upon whom shall My Spirit rest? Even upon him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at My words.” Dost thou wish to be a place for the Lord? Be thou poor in spirit, and contrite, and trembling at the word of God, and thou wilt thyself be made what thou seekest. For if what thou seekest be not realized in thyself, what doth it profit thee in another.…

Wherefore if we wish the summit of our building to be perfect and to rise well-pleasing to God, we should endeavour to lay its foundations not in accordance with the desires of our own lust, but according to the rules of evangelical strictness: which can only be the fear of God and humility, proceeding from kindness and simplicity of heart. But humility cannot possibly be acquired without giving up everything: and as long as a man is a stranger to this, he cannot possibly attain the virtue of obedience, or the strength of patience, or the serenity of kindness, or the perfection of love; without which things our hearts cannot possibly be a habitation for the Holy Spirit: as the Lord says through the prophet: "Upon whom shall My spirit rest, but on him that is humble and quiet and ears My words," or according to those copies which express the Hebrew accurately: "To whom shall I have respect, but to him that is poor and little and of a contrite spirit and that trembleth at My words?"
The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 12, Chapter 31

In these terms God rejects the worship that was restricted to one place and shows that he is the maker of heaven and earth, and the shaper of all things and the one who has no need of a temple made with hands... I have a true house and holy temple. It is whoever arranges his or her life according to my laws and fears and trembles at transgressing my commands. It is the person who stands out in a gentle disposition and humility of mind.
People do not observe a spiritual sabbath unless they devote themselves to earthly occupations so moderately that they still engage in reading and prayer, at least frequently, if not always.

God wishes to dwell in you. In order that you may not be unable to receive him because you are full, if you are filled elsewhere, let your heart be freed of superfluities so that it may be filled with what is necessary. Vices should be expelled, in order that there may be room for virtues; to say briefly what is useful and quite necessary, let carnal desires be rejected and charity invited. As long as we do not expel evil, we cannot be filled with the good, because jars filled with slime cannot receive and hold precious ointment.

Differently to be admonished are the humble and the haughty. To the former it is to be insinuated how true is that excellence which they hold in hoping for it; to the latter it is to be intimated how that temporal glory is as nothing which even when embracing it they hold not. Let the humble hear how eternal are the things that they long for, how transitory the things which they despise; let the haughty hear how transitory are the things they court, how eternal the things they lose. Let the humble hear from the authoritative voice of the Truth, Every one that humbleth himself shall be exalted. Let the haughty hear, Every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled. Let the humble hear, Humility goeth before glory; let the haughty hear, The spirit is exalted before a fall. Let the humble hear, Unto whom shall I have respect, but to him that is humble and quiet, and that trembleth at my words?
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 3, Chapter 17

The first benefit of the fear of God is that the fear of God avails for obtaining the influx of divine grace. Whence Isaiah: "To whom shall I look, except to the poor and contrite of spirit and the one trembling at my words?" However powerful, rich, learned, and strong a man may be, unless he fears God, nothing avails him.

Grace makes a man pleasing to God: but he is pleasing to God who recognizes the gift of divine favor and condescension: yet no one recognizes this except one who is attentive to his own unworthiness: and such a one is truly humble: and hence it is that the grace of the Holy Spirit rests upon the humble alone. Whence in the last chapter of Isaiah: Upon whom does My Spirit rest if not upon the humble, etc.
Disputed Questions on Evangelical Perfection, Question 1

And he gives a useful remedy: but to whom shall I have respect, but to him that is poor and little, that is, the humble man, who reckons himself to be little, as to the present, and of a contrite spirit, concerning his past sins, and that trembles, as to his intention of doing future things: the eyes of the Lord are towards them that fear him (Sir 15:20[19]).

The work of a man who has murmured or has been detected in pride must not be mixed with that done by men humble in heart and of a contrite spirit; it must not be used at all by the pious. “For that which is exalted among men is an abomination before God.” And there is another command of the apostle: “Neither murmur ye, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer.” Then there is this: “Not grudgingly or of necessity.” So the work of such men is unacceptable, like a blemished sacrifice—which it was impious to mingle with the offerings of other men. For if those who brought strange fire to the altar experienced such great wrath, surely it is perilous to accept a work springing from a mind hostile to God to assist us in keeping God’s commandments. “For what fellowship have righteousness and iniquity? Or what portion hath a believer with an unbeliever?” Wherefore it saith: “The lawless, he that sacrificeth a calf for me, is as he that killeth a dog; and he that bringeth a meal offering is as he that bringeth swine’s blood.” Wherefore the works of the hesitating and gainsaying man are to be removed from the brotherhood.

All these things they have chosen in their ways, and in their abominations their soul has delighted. Therefore I too will choose their mockeries, and what they feared I will bring upon them. For I called, and there was none to answer: I spoke, and they did not hear: and they did evil in my eyes: and what I did not will, they chose. LXX: And they themselves have chosen their ways, and their soul has willed their abominations: and I will choose their mockeries, and repay them their sins. For I called them, and they did not hearken: I spoke, and they did not hear. And they did evil in my sight, and what I did not will they chose. To sacrifice an ox, to slaughter a ram, to offer sacrifice, to burn frankincense, which God regards as murder and the offering of a dog, and swine's blood and blasphemy, they themselves chose; and that they should worship such things was of their own choice; according to what he says through Ezekiel: I gave them statutes not good, and precepts not good (Ezek 20:25). And in their own ways, he says, they walked, not in the way of the Lord. And their soul has willed their abominations, so that they were lovers of themselves rather than lovers of God. For this reason, since they chose their own ways, and not him who says: I am the way (John 14:6), the Lord too chose their mockeries, or their mockers, who in Hebrew are called THALULE (תעללי), that is, ἐμπαῖκται, so as to set over them very wicked princes, and bring upon them likewise all their evils, or what they feared. And he gives the reasons why they were handed over to the Scribes and Pharisees, their mockers, of whom the first psalm sings according to the Hebrews: And he has not sat in the chair of the mockers: whom the Seventy call the pestilent: such as were the sons of Eli, sons of pestilence, for which in the Hebrew BELIAL (בליעל) is written, that is, of the devil. For, he says, I called, and there was none to answer: I spoke, and they did not hear: and they did evil in my eyes: and what I did not will, they chose. These verses he sets down a second time in the present place, and also above, where it is said: I will number you for the sword, and you shall all fall in the slaughter: for I called, and you did not answer (Isa 65:12), and the rest likewise. In what sense this testimony ought to be taken was said there.

And what follows in the common edition: But the wicked man, is not found in the Hebrew, but it simply joins on and says: He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man. This is also written in another place: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice: the knowledge of God rather than holocaust (Hos 6:6). And through Malachi: All that I hated, you did: covering my altar with tears: is it fitting that I should look upon your sacrifice, and receive anything acceptable from your hands (Mal 2:13)? Let the Jews hear that God does not seek sacrifices, but the mind of those who offer. And he who slaughters, he says, a sheep is as one who brains a dog. Hence it is also written through Moses: You shall not offer the hire of a harlot, nor the price of a dog, in the house of your God. (Deut 23:18). And the dog and the harlot are fittingly joined, because each animal is prone to lust. And at the same time let us consider that he did not say: He who sacrifices a ram is as one who sacrifices a dog; but as one who kills, he says, a dog. This word is not used of sacrifices, but of things that are slaughtered unlawfully. He who offers an oblation and sacrifice is as one who offers swine's blood. This too is itself forbidden by the Law; such are the ceremonies of the Jews (Lev 11, and Deut 14). He who gives frankincense is as a blasphemer, or rather as one who blesses an idol. But this too may be the sense: After my Son, who came meek and poor, sitting upon the colt of an ass, I do not want flesh, I detest victims, I reject the sacrifices of the Jews and the shadows of the Law, because the truth of the Gospel is delightful to me (Zech 9, and Matt 21, and Luke 19, and John 12). But if this is said, that after the lightning of the Gospel the old religion ceases in the cloud, what will they answer who, believing from among the Jews, think that they can offer sacrifices carnally without harm to themselves?

By these words he rejected the worship prescribed by the law by teaching this; it was for their sake that he had established this legislation from early times, not because he took pleasure in their sacrifices but because he was exercising forethought for them in their weakness. That is why he put side by side what was allowed and what was forbidden, for to sacrifice an ox or give a sheep as a burnt offering, to offer the fruit of corn and frankincense—these were in former times permitted by God, but to start a fight and lose one's tongue to blasphemy was totally forbidden.

Second, he excludes the confidence that they took from their rites of sacrifice. And first, he sets out their rejection: he that sacrifices an ox, is as if he slew a man, as if to say: their sacrifices are so abominable, as if they were doing something against the law, because they were offering them to idols; as if he should bless, praise and venerate, an idol, above: offer sacrifice no more in vain (Isa 1:13). Second, he shows the reason for their rejection, first, setting out their fault: all these things have they chosen, namely, their sacrifices, walking in their wicked ways: who are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in the most wicked things (Prov 2:14).

Second, he threatens punishment: wherefore I also will choose their mockeries: he shall scorn the scorners (Prov 3:34); the fear which I feared, has come upon me: and that which I was afraid of, has befallen me (Job 3:25). Third, he denounces the hardness of sinners: because I called: I called, and you refused (Prov 1:24).

Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his speech. Your brothers who hate you, and cast you out for my name's sake, have said: Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see in your gladness: but they shall be put to shame. LXX: Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his speech. Say to your brothers who hate you and abhor you, that the name of the Lord may be glorified: and may it appear in their gladness: and they shall be put to shame. Those of whom he had already said before: Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words? he commands that, having despised the victims of the Jews and scorned all the swelling pride of the Scribes and Pharisees, they pass over to the worship of him whom those others would not hear when he called, and despised, and did evil in his sight. Nor is he content with this end of his precepts, but he enjoins on them the commandment of the Gospel (Luke 6): that they love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, and pray for their persecutors, and imitate the mercy of the Father, who makes his sun rise upon the just and the unjust: That seeing, he says, your works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt 5:16). After the general understanding, this is commanded specially to the Apostles and to apostolic men: that they love the Jews, their persecutors, and hold those who abhor them in the place of brothers, saying with Peter: Men, brothers and fathers, hear; and with the apostle Paul: I have sadness, and continual sorrow in my heart, for my brothers who are Israelites (Rom 9:2). And the name of the Lord is glorified when men see the ferocity of persecutors broken by our patience, and the striking hand put to shame by the turning of the other cheek. To these it is commanded in the Gospel: Let your light shine before men, that seeing your good works they may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt 5:16); and in the Apocalypse of John: Fear God, and give him glory (Rev 14:7). Paul too writes to the Corinthians, calling them to continence: That you may glorify God in your body (1 Cor 6:20). And again: Whether you eat or drink, do all to the glory of God (1 Cor 10:31). Hence the Lord too did not curse in return those who cursed him (1 Pet 2), and prayed for his persecutors. But what he commands: Say to your brothers (Matt 28:10), is not to be taken simply; otherwise many call others brothers and do not keep love in their heart, of whom the Apostle writes: They profess that they know God, but in their works they deny him (Titus 1:16). Of these the Lord too was speaking: Not everyone who says to me: Lord, Lord, shall enter the kingdom of heaven: but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven (Matt 7:21). And so that sentence can stand: No one says, Lord Jesus, except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 12:3). For though the heretics say Lord Jesus, and many in the resurrection will say: Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and do many mighty works (Matt 7:22)? the Lord will answer them: Depart from me, I do not know you, workers of iniquity. Therefore saying is proved not by speech, which is easy, but by disposition and works. From these things we learn that the Lord of both Testaments is the same, who commands that if we see the beast of our enemy fall under its burden, we should not pass by, but lift it up with him, and if we find an ox or an ass straying, we should return it to him (Luke 15, Matt 18). So much according to the Seventy. Further, according to the Hebrew, this seems to me to be the sense: Hear, Apostles, hear, my disciples, you who tremble at the word of the Lord: I will tell what your brothers have said, who hate and separate you and reckon you strangers, not because of your evils but because of my name; who think unclean all those of their nation who believe in me, and say: Depart from me, for you are unclean. What, then, is it that he records them to have said: Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see in your gladness? The sense of this little verse is this: Why do you bring in to us a humble God? why one crucified, and a man of sorrows, who knows how to bear infirmities? We want to behold him reigning in his majesty (as you say): we will look up to him triumphing in his glory too; humble and cast down we cannot see him. And at once he adds: But they shall be put to shame; understood: those who say such things, who do not understand the mysteries of the Scriptures, and will feel through their own evils the power of him whom they had despised for his humility.

"Your brothers who hate you." Consider them as your brothers, he says, even though they hate you because of your faith, and lead them to the fear of God, so that "the Lord may be glorified in you." According to Henana, consider them to be execrable and evil, he says, even though they are your brothers by nature. "When they are cast out for my name, the Lord will be glorified" in you, "and they will be put to shame," and maybe, he says, they will be put to shame because of that and will abstain from evil actions.

Hear the word of the Lord. Here he describes the manner of execution of the sentence. And first, as to the rewards of the good; second, as to the punishments of the wicked: and the hand of the Lord shall be known (Isa 66:14). The first of these is divided into two. First, he stirs up attention: hear the word of the Lord, you that tremble, from reverence for his words: you that fear the Lord, believe him (Sir 2:8); second, he describes the promise. And first, as to vengeance on the mockers, setting out their mockery: your brethren have said: let the Lord be glorified, as if to say: let the glory of the Lord, which you await, appear, as if to say: he will never appear, above: they shall come with speed swiftly, and there is none that shall faint, nor labor among them (Isa 5:26–27); and he foretells their confusion: but they shall be confounded.

A voice of uproar from the city, a voice from the Temple, the voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies. For uproar the LXX put crying, and the rest likewise. We wish to know what the confusion of the Jews is, who said: Let the Lord be glorified, that we may see your gladness, and may behold the triumphs of your king with our eyes, by no means in empty promises. A voice, he says, of crying from the city: without doubt it signifies Jerusalem surrounded by the Roman army and divided within into three parts by sedition, when one held the Temple and possessed all that had formerly been holy, fighting outside against the enemy and inside against his fellow citizens. At that time, both in the city and in the Temple, there was heard the howling of priests and Levites as well as of the common rabble, of women and children, when the Lord rendered recompense to his enemies, fulfilling the threat in which he had said: Your house shall be left to you desolate (Luke 13:35); and that prophecy: I have forsaken my house. When the Angels presiding over the temple said with one voice: Let us pass out of these abodes. Of these things not only Josephus, the writer of the Jewish history, but many ages before the Psalmist testifies, saying: I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city (Ps 54 [55]:10), which surrounded its walls all day and all night, so that the city was overthrown (Mic 3), and another prophecy was fulfilled: Zion shall be plowed like a field: and Jerusalem shall be left like a hut in a garden of cucumbers (Isa 1:8).

For it was the Lord's voice that said, "rendering recompense to his enemies," ordering and exhorting those who destroy to spare none of those captured, savagely attacking the enemies and not only simply with the wrath of warriors but also with the will of the Sovereign. For this was only the means of their captivity and suffering.
In this manner, because a voice of the people, fearing, the voice of the Lord, as to the tumult of their enemies: the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter (Zeph 1:14).

Now that that parturition was polluted, and stood not in need of expiatory victims, Isaiah is our witness, who proclaims distinctly to the whole earth under the sun: "Before she travailed," he says, "she brought forth before her pains came, she escaped, and brought forth a man-child." Who hath heard such a thing? Who hath seen such things? The most holy virgin mother, therefore, escaped entirely the manner of women even before she brought forth: doubtless, in order that the Holy Spirit, betrothing her unto Himself, and sanctifying her, she might conceive without intercourse with man. She hath brought forth her first-born Son, even the only-begotten Son of God, Him, I say, who in the heavens above shone forth as the only-begotten, without mother, from out His Father's substance, and preserved the virginity of His natural unity undivided and inseparable; and who on earth, in the virgin's nuptial chamber, joined to Himself the nature of Adam, like a bridegroom, by an inalienable union, and preserved His mother's purity uncorrupt and uninjured—Him, in short, who in heaven was begotten without corruption, and on earth brought forth in a manner quite unspeakable.

Before she was in labor, she brought forth: before her travail came, she brought forth a male. Who has ever heard such a thing? who has seen the like of this ? Shall the earth be in labor in one day: or shall a nation be brought forth at once? for Zion has been in labor and has brought forth her sons: Shall I, who make others bring forth, not bring forth myself, says the Lord? If I, who give generation to the rest, am barren, says the Lord your God. LXX: Before she who travails brings forth: before the pain of those in travail comes, she escapes, and she has brought forth a male. Who has heard such a thing, and who has seen the like? If the earth has travailed in one day; or if a nation has been born at once, because Zion has travailed and brought forth her little ones. But I have given this expectation, and you have not remembered me, says the Lord. Have I not made her who bears and the barren, says your God? While the crying resounded from Jerusalem and its Temple, when it was besieged and overthrown, and the enemies of Christ, who would not receive God as king, were receiving eternal punishments for their impiety and blasphemies, the Church gathered in the name of the Lord, of which it is said in the psalm: A man was born in her: and the most high himself has founded her (Ps 86 [87]:5), before she was in labor brought forth; before her travail came, she bore a male. For it was not over a long time, as the people of the Jews grew greater through Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the twelve Patriarchs, and again through their children and grandchildren; but at the preaching of the Gospel the whole world at once conceived, and was in labor, and brought forth a male, whom Pharaoh and Herod tried to kill, and who, both in Moses and in Christ, was saved in Egypt. Finally, Abraham and Isaac had male children, and Jacob, the father of many sons, begot one daughter, for whose sake he suffered hard things (Gen 34). And if the daughters of Zelophehad, by the sentence of God, receive their father's inheritance (Num 27), this is to be considered: that their father, who begot no son, died in his own sin, and that Moses dared to judge nothing concerning them, but referred it to the Lord, who, lest they remain without means, commanded them to be joined to their kinsmen. The book of Genesis also relates (Chapter 6) that after men began to become many, a number that is always associated with vice, and daughters were born to them, they were taken, not by Angels, but by the sons of God, from whom the giants were born: or, as it is written in the Hebrew, ἐπιπίπτοντες, that is, those who fall upon. On the contrary, it is said to the saint: Your wife like an abundant vine on the sides of your house. Your sons like young olive plants round about your table (Ps 127 [128]:3). And again: May you see your sons' sons (ibid. 6).

Again Isaiah teaches that Jerusalem will not be destroyed root, branch and all. For when he foretold the complete captivity of Jerusalem, he mentioned those chosen to survive. For a not insignificant number will be saved, obviously through faith in Christ—and he wants to make this clear. But the Jews were enraged with him and killed the prince of life. But when he rose again, trampling on death, he returned to his God and Father in heaven. In the meantime, the divine apostles proclaimed him to all, and they called even those who had been enraged with him to repentance and to salvation through faith and the forgiveness of sins through baptism.

For He who was of the Father, yet without mother, was born of woman without a father’s co-operation. And so far as He was born of woman, His birth was in accordance with the laws of parturition, while so far as He had no father, His birth was above the nature of generation: and in that it was at the usual time (for He was born on the completion of the ninth month when the tenth was just beginning), His birth was in accordance with the laws of parturition, while in that it was painless it was above the laws of generation. For, as pleasure did not precede it, pain did not follow it, according to the prophet who says, Before she travailed, she brought forth, and again, before her pain came she was delivered of a man-child.
An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 14

Second, he describes the promise as to abundance of goods. And first, as to the reuniting of the people, setting out the promise, before she was in labor, she brought forth; that is, the children of Jerusalem will be gathered to her suddenly and at the same time, just as if a woman brought forth a child suddenly, without first being in labor, above: the children are come to the birth (Isa 37:3). Mystically, this is interpreted as concerning the labor of the Blessed Virgin, and the labor of the Church in the conversion of the faithful, and the labor of eternal begetting.

It is admitted that when in recent times the appearance of our Saviour Jesus Christ had become known to all men there immediately made its appearance a new nation; a nation confessedly not small, and not dwelling in some corner of the earth, but the most numerous and pious of all nations, indestructible and unconquerable, because it always receives assistance from God. This nation, thus suddenly appearing at the time appointed by the inscrutable counsel of God, is the one which has been honored by all with the name of Christ.

One of the prophets, when he saw beforehand with the eye of the Divine Spirit that which was to be, was so astonished at it that he cried out, "Who hath heard of such things, and who hath spoken thus? Hath the earth brought forth in one day, and hath a nation been born at once?" And the same prophet gives a hint also of the name by which the nation was to be called, when he says, "Those that serve me shall be called by a new name, which shall be blessed upon the earth."

But for God this was no great thing, that the dead should be quickened. Before seed was sown in the earth, the earth produced that which had not been cast into it. Before it had conceived, it bore in its virginity. How then is this difficult, that the earth should cause to spring up again what had been cast into it, and after conception should bear? And lo! her travail-pains are near; as Isaiah said, Who hath seen anything like this and who hath heard such things as these? that the earth should travail in one day, and a people should be born in one hour? For Adam unsown sprang up; unconceived he was born. But lo! now his offspring are sown, and wait for the rain, and shall spring up. And lo! the earth teems with many, and the time of her bringing forth is at hand.
Demonstration 8 (Of the Resurrection of the Dead), Section 6

Further, according to the LXX the sense is this: that at one time, at the preaching of the Gospels, one nation of the whole world should arise. Through many prophets I have often promised, and you have not remembered my promise, O city which is full of cries, O Temple which has been forsaken by the Lord, O people to whom I have rendered its recompense. Have I not, he says, made her who travails and the barren; she who before had been barren afterwards travailed and brought forth? Of her it is written in the psalm: Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a mother rejoicing in sons (Ps 112 [113]:9). Or certainly the order of things has been reversed: she who bore has become barren, and she who was once barren has brought forth very many, because this is the sentence of the Lord.

Zion, then, that is, the remnant from Israel and the faith of the believing Apostles, brought forth a male, the Lord Savior, who was born at once in the whole world: something that no one has heard of, that no history relates, nor the teaching of anyone, that all the nations should believe in a short time, and that out of all the nations there should be made one nation of the Christians, of which Paul too speaks: If anyone is a new creature in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, they have become new (2 Cor 5:17): according to what is written elsewhere: And all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight: for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations. For all the nations, he says, which you have made shall come and worship before you, and shall glorify your name (Ps 21 [22]:28ff.). Of him Jacob says: He is the expectation of the nations (Gen 49:10). And the Psalmist: The hope of all the ends of the earth (Ps 64 [65]:6). And the same Isaiah whom we are now expounding: There shall be the root of Jesse, and he who shall rise up to be prince of the nations; in him the nations shall hope (Isa 11:10); the Apostles fulfilling what was commanded: Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19), so that a new people may be born, of which Psalm 21 (22) also sings: The heavens shall announce his righteousness to a people that shall be born, which the Lord has made (Ps 21 [22]:32). And again: A people that shall be created shall praise the Lord (Ps 101 [102]:19). And this people was created in one day, which the sun of righteousness illumines, as Scripture says: The Lord shall be to you an everlasting light (Isa 60:19). What is said: A nation shall arise at once, for Zion has been in labor and has brought forth her sons, we can also refer to that time when in one day three thousand and five thousand of the Jewish people believed (Acts 2). It is also said in the same book of the Acts of the Apostles that there were in Jerusalem men from all the nations under heaven, who heard them speaking the great works of God in various tongues (ibid.).
And he introduces the wondering question: who has ever heard such a thing, above: who has begotten these? (Isa 49:21).

And what follows according to the LXX: But I have given this expectation, and you have not remembered me, says the Lord. Have I not made her who bears and the barren, said your God, is put more plainly in the Hebrew, with which the other translators also agree: Shall I, who make others bring forth, not bring forth myself, says the Lord? If I, who give generation to the rest, am barren, says the Lord your God; according to what is said elsewhere: He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? and he who formed the eye, does he not consider (Ps 93 [94]:9); namely, that he who created all men out of nothing can make out of all the nations one part of those who believe in him, the Church. Finally, in Psalm 28 (29), where we read: The voice of the Lord shaking the desert (Ps 28 [29]:8), in the Hebrew it is written: The voice of the Lord making the desert bring forth (According to the Hebrew), so that the Church, formerly a desert, may bring forth, and the stags may be perfected when the woodlands are opened and crushed.

To that which is objected, that the cause of generation and corruption is to be far distant from the First: it must be said that this is not the whole reason. For man, if he had remained in the state of innocence, would never have been corrupted, and yet he would have generated. Whence generation is rather from the supreme perfection and fecundity and actuality of the first principle itself, than it is for the supplementing of the defect of corruption of the productive principle itself. Therefore the Philosopher speaks of the cause of generation according to the state of deficient nature, not generally and according to the mode of that most complete generation, which is the origin of all production. For the generator of the species constituted all these things, and he himself, who bestows generation upon others, cannot be sterile, according to what is said in the last chapter of Isaiah.
Quaestiones Disputatae, De Mysterio Trinitatis, Question 6

And he sets out the response in the person of the Lord: shall not I that make others to bring forth children, myself bring forth, gathering the Jews, or the converted faithful; or the Son, from eternity. Similar to this is Psalm 93[94]:9: he that planted the ear, shall he not hear? Or he that formed the eye, doth he not consider? And these arguments hold, if that which belongs to the perfection of creatures is attributed [to God], removing all that which belongs to imperfection.

Rejoice with Jerusalem, and exult in her, all you who love her. Rejoice with her with joy, all you who mourn over her, that you may suck and be filled from the breast of her consolation, that you may milk and abound with delights from her glory of every kind. LXX: Rejoice, Jerusalem, and make an assembly, all you who love her. Rejoice with joy, all you who mourn over her, that you may suck and be filled from the breast of her consolation, that, after you have sucked, you may be delighted from the entrance of her glory. It is commanded to the Apostles and to apostolic men, who love both Jerusalems, bewailing and mourning the one that has fallen, and awaiting with all desire the one that is to rise, that they rejoice with her and in her, who has been built of living stones, which roll upon the earth and, in the likeness of the wheels of the Cherubim, follow the spirit going before: not in those stones which have been dissolved into eternal ashes. Of these the Lord was speaking: Amen, amen I say to you, there shall not remain stone upon stone, until all these things are fulfilled (Matt 24:2). Rejoice, he says, with her with joy, all you who mourn her. Such were those whom we have shown above, the apostles Peter and Paul, and all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel: that they may suck and be filled at the breasts of her consolation.

Second, he promises immense comfort to the gathered Jews. And first, he invites others to congratulation: rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, as in the object of joy, setting out the condition of congratulation as to affection: all you that love her: eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved (Song 5:1); as to the sign of affection: all you that mourn for her: blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:5).

For it could not be that she who had borne a male and had just given birth should lack an abundance of milk for the rearing of that nation and of the little ones who had been born at once, so that she might offer them two breasts, by no means, as formerly in Egypt, broken and lying low, but whole and standing in virginal beauty, those of the Old and New Instrument, to supply rational milk. Of these the bridegroom speaks to her: Your breasts are better than wine (Song 1:1). These were the ones of whom they specially said: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:5). And this is to be noted: that those who are little ones need the milk of consolation, and are still in a mortal place. But those who after the milk of consolation have advanced to solid food will abound with the delights of truth, and with the knowledge of glory of every kind, which in Hebrew is called ZIZ (זיז). For this the LXX translated entrance; Symmachus fatness; Theodotion multitude. We have said this in order to open an ambiguous word of Psalm 79 (80), in which it is written: The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it (Ps 79 [80]:14). For where in our codices and in the Greek one reads μόνιος ἄγριος, that is, the solitary wild beast, in the Hebrew ZIZ SADAI (זיז שדי) is written: which Aquila translated παντόδαπον χώρας, that is, every kind of thing of the region, to signify that Israel was laid waste not only by the Romans but by all the nations. And the glorious entrance of the Church is to be understood as that of which the apostle John writes: And in the twelve gates were twelve pearls, and the streets of the city of pure gold, like transparent glass (Rev 21:21). These pearls the Lord forbids to be cast before swine (Matt 7); and when the good merchant has found them in the Prophets and Apostles, he goes on to the one most precious pearl, not casting away the former ones, but seeking through them the more precious (Matt 13).

This struggle is the correction of noble good deeds in them. For their sweat is profitable, and they have youth-like endurance in order to gain not an earthly possession but rather so that they become filled with graces from God and are satisfied in every desire. To these he makes this promise, "Like infants at the breast you will be filled by the breasts of consolation." Since Isaiah has previously compared the figure of a woman with the new Zion, he remains in this way of speaking and compares this comfort with that of the breasts and milk of the Holy Spirit. For in the Song of Songs it says, "Your breasts are better than wine."

And the fruit of congratulation as to participation in her gladness or peace: that you may suck: your breasts are better than wine (Song 1:1); as to participation in her glory, that you may milk out, as though extracting milk: then shall you abound in delights in the Almighty (Job 22:6).

So, then, the Holy Spirit is the river, and the abundant river, which according to the Hebrews flowed from Jesus in the lands, as we have received it prophesied by the mouth of Isaiah. This is the great river that flows always and never fails. And not only a river but also one of the copious stream and overflowing greatness, as also David said, "The stream of the river makes glad the city of God."

For thus says the Lord: Behold, I turn upon her as it were a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent the glory of the nations, which you shall suck: you shall be carried at the breast, and upon the knees they shall caress you. LXX: For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent overflowing the glory of the nations. Their little ones shall be carried on the shoulders, and upon the knees they shall be comforted. When Jerusalem has been built up by the Apostles and restored to her former state, after her sons and inhabitants have been comforted at her breasts and through the abundance of milk have come to the delights of truth, through which one comes to the glory of God: then the Lord will turn upon her the river of peace, of which we have often said: The river of God is filled with waters (Ps 64 [65]:10). And: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:5); so that, with peace possessing all things, and the wars of the nations ceasing, of whom Scripture says: Scatter the nations that want wars (Ps 67 [68]:32), the torrent of the teachings of God may water the fields of believers. Then her sons, or little ones (as the LXX translated), shall be carried on the shoulders, and upon the knees they shall receive comfort. On the shoulders, of which it was also said in the earlier prophecy, and which Jacob invokes upon his son Issachar: For he put his shoulder under to labor (Gen 49:15), and he was called a husbandman. For it is by sweat and great labor that we come to an abundance of fruits. Hence it is said to Zion through Jeremiah too: Set your heart upon your shoulders (Jer 24:7), so that she may understand the Lord from his commandments, imitating him of whom it is written: Jesus began to do and to teach (Acts 1:1), so that faith may not be idle, but may run through works to the reward. What knees and bosom signify I have briefly explained above too, and now the example of Abraham can teach us, in whose bosom Lazarus rests, and all who come from the East and the West, who shall recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

And Scripture calls Christ "glory," for the psalmist says about him, "to prepare glory in our land." This entrance is the mystery of the economy in the flesh. Being God by nature, he became man through his incarnation and in such manner came into the world. Those feed on the precise message of faith concerning him, and they learn in what way the glory, that is, Christ came into the world. And directly connected to this, the divine prophet speaks of his clear appearance in the flesh, taking on Christ's voice as he says, "I will descend on them as a river of peace, and as a spring I will wash over the glory of the nations."

Second, he promises an abundant gathering of peace: for thus says the Lord: behold I will bring upon her, so that an overflowing is called, as a river descending with great force comes and does not overflow; and of glory: and as an overflowing torrent, above: your peace had been as a river (Isa 48:18).

Third, he promises full reception of comfort. First, as to the administration of the gentiles: which you shall suck, that is, the glory of the Gentiles, for the kings of the gentiles themselves will comfort and sustain you; thus follows: at the breasts. Mystically: this is said of the Apostles, who delighted in the glory of the gentiles who were swiftly converted, and who carried them as at the breast with caressing admonitions, above: you shall suck the milk of the Gentiles (Isa 60:16).

A mother draws her children near her; we seek our mother, the church. Whatever is weak and young has an appeal and sweetness and lovableness of its own, just because in its weakness it does stand in need of assistance. But God does not withhold assistance from such an age of life. Just as the male and female parent regard their young tenderly—whether it be horses their colts, or cows their calves, or lions their cubs, or deer their fawn or men and women their children—so, too, does the Father of all draw near to those who seek his aid, giving them a new birth and making them his own adopted children. He recognizes them as his little ones, he loves only them, and he comes to the aid of such as these and defends them. That is why he calls them his children.

As one whom a mother caresses, so will I comfort you, and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted. You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall sprout like grass. And the hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall be indignant with his enemies. For servants the LXX put those who fear; for enemies, the unbelieving: the rest likewise. We learn the mercy of the Creator toward his creatures from the example of mothers, who, nursing their children with love in their bosom, surpass every affection. Finally, God, wishing to show how he loves those whom he has created: Shall, he says, a woman forget, so as not to have pity on the offspring of her womb? but even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you (Isa 49:15). The Gospel passage too has this sense, in which the Lord speaks to Jerusalem: How often have I wished to gather your sons, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not (Matt 23:37)? And Deuteronomy, in which something of the kind resounds: As the eagle protects her nest, and has longed for her young: spreading her wings, she has taken them up and carried them on her shoulders (Deut 32:11). Those who have written on the natures of living creatures say that in all wild beasts, beasts of burden, cattle and birds there is an inborn affection toward their offspring and young, but that the love of eagles is the greatest, which place their nests in high and inaccessible places, lest a snake harm the brood. And that an amethyst stone is found among its young, by which all poisons are overcome. If this is true, the affection of God toward his creatures is rightly compared to eagles, who protects his children with every guard, lest the dragon and ancient snake, the devil and Satan, creep up on the new brood, so that at the name of the stone which is laid in the foundations of Zion all the snares of the adversaries may be broken. And this Jerusalem, in which the sons shall be comforted by their mother and fondled on her knees, is the one of which the Apostle writes: But the Jerusalem that is above is free, which is the mother of us all (Gal 4:26). Filled with the milk of her consolation, he comforted the others who needed his words, saying: Blessed be God, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who comforts us in all tribulation, so that we too may be able to comfort those who are in any tribulation, through the consolation with which we ourselves are comforted by God (2 Cor 1:3).
Second, as to divine protection: as one whom the mother caresses: you have forgotten the consolation (Heb 12:5).

After these have been comforted, it will be said to them: And you shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall sprout like grass, or shall spring up, or according to Symmachus, shall flourish (John 16:22). And they shall see, without doubt, God, which is true gladness. Of these the Lord spoke: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). The vision of him is perfect joy, which dwells in the heart of full faith: and the sprouting of the bones follows, of which we have already spoken before. If the reader has forgotten this, let him go back to the earlier explanation. For it is better for him to read again what was written than for us to repeat what was said. And known, he says, shall be the hand of the Lord to his servants, or to those who fear him, and he shall threaten his enemies, or his unbelieving. Now the hand is taken either for power, in that God can do all the things that he promises, according to what Moses says in the person of God to Pharaoh: Now I will send forth my hand, and I will strike you, and I will kill your people, and you shall be blotted out from the earth (Exod 3:20). And again he himself to the same tyrant: Behold, the hand of the Lord shall be upon your cattle (Exod 9:4); of which the Psalmist said to God: Your hand slew the nations, and you planted them (Ps 43 [44]). Or certainly the hand of the Lord is to be understood as Christ, of whom we also read above: My hand has made all these things. This hand the Lord will make known to his servants and to those who fear him, and he will threaten his unbelieving ones and his enemies, so as to promise rewards to the one, and to threaten punishments to the other. In this the propriety of the words is to be considered: that he did not say, He will inflict upon his enemies, but he shall threaten, so that, deterred by the threat, they too may pass over to the service of the Lord.

For it is not only in the present life that I provide consolation for you through my heralds, but also in the heavenly city I will fill you with manifold joys—granting you the resurrection from the dead. This is what he meant by comparing the growth of bones to the growth of a plant.

Third, as to the enjoyment of goods, you shall see good things given to you by God; bones, you who in adversity were like dry bones: you dry bones, hear the word of the Lord (Ezek 37:4). Or you shall see the divine essence: the light is sweet, and it is delightful for the eyes to see the sun (Eccl 11:7); and your bones shall flourish like an herb, in the resurrection.

And the hand of the Lord shall be known. Here he promises punishment to the wicked. And first, he threatens punishment, setting out the indignation of the judge: the hand, afflicting the impious, in his servants; or, the hand, of comfort, in his servants, by its effect, above: there is no indignation in me (Isa 27:4).

[Passage quoted, Isa. lxvi. 18, 19.]

HERE also the Coming of the Lord to men is exactly foretold. And as it said, "He will come as fire," our Saviour rightly says, "I came to cast fire on the earth, and what will I, if it be already kindled?" You may say His "chariots" are His attendant divine powers, and the holy angels chosen to minister to Him, of whom it is said, "and angels came and ministered to Him," and His holy apostles and disciples, borne up by whom, the Word of God with divine invisible power ran through all the world. One might also literally in another way connect fire and chariots with His coming, through the siege that attacked Jerusalem after our Saviour's Advent, for the Temple was burned with fire not long after, and was reduced to extreme desolation, and the city was encircled by the chariots and camps of the enemy, after which too the promises to the Gentiles were fulfilled in harmony with the prophecy.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 25

For behold, the Lord will come in fire: and his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his fury in indignation, and his rebuke in a flame of fire. For in fire the Lord is judged, and with his sword unto all flesh: and those slain by the Lord shall be multiplied. LXX: Behold, the Lord will come as fire, and his chariots as a tempest, to render his vengeance in fury: and his rebuke in a flame of fire. For in the fire of the Lord all the earth shall be judged: and by his sword all flesh shall fall: many shall be wounded by the Lord. The hand of the Lord, which will be made known to his servants and to those who fear him, itself threatens the unbelieving, or his enemies, that if they do not repent they shall endure what follows: For behold, he says, the Lord will come in fire, and his chariots like a whirlwind or tempest. These we ought to understand as the Angelic powers, when the Lord is to come in the glory of the Father with his Angels, to judge the living and the dead: not that the Lord is fire, but that to those who endure punishments he seems to be fire. And although Moses said (Deut 4:24), and the Apostle confirms the same (Heb 12:29): God is a consuming fire; yet the Savior, expressing the substance of the divinity, says: God is spirit (John 4:24). But between spirit and fire, according to bodily understanding, there is much difference. And if he is fire or spirit, how is he said to have eyes and ears and hands and feet and belly and the other members of the body, since spirit and fire do not have these? God, then, is called a consuming fire so that he may consume whatever vices are in us, hay, wood and stubble, and the thorns, that is, the cares of this world, which the unfruitful earth has borne instead of good seed, of which it is said to the Hebrews: But that which bears thorns and thistles is reprobate and near to a curse; whose end is burning (Heb 6:8). Of this fire the Lord too was speaking in the Gospel: I have come to cast fire upon the earth (Luke 12:49). And we read above: Iniquity shall burn like fire, and like dry grass it shall be consumed by fire (Isa 9:18), and all the tares which the enemy sowed over, while the householder slept (Matt 13). Of this it is also written in the Epistle of James: How small a fire kindles how great a matter (Jas 3:5)! And in Proverbs: With much wood the fire thrives (Prov 26:20). Although, in that it is a proverb, something else may be understood (Sir 28). This fire, I think, sat upon the tongues of the Apostles and of all believers, when they spoke in various tongues, and it put to flight all the darkness of error, and illuminated the hearts of those who received the word of the Lord (Acts 2). And what follows: His chariots like a tempest, or his four-horse chariots, we shall explain by examples from the Psalms, in which it is written: God will come openly, our God, and will not keep silent. Fire shall burn before him: and round about him a mighty tempest (Ps 49 [50]:3, 4). And elsewhere: The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those who rejoice (Ps 67 [68]:18). With these chariots and horses Elisha was surrounded, which his servant could not see. Hence he says: O Lord, open the eyes of this servant, that he may see. And when his eyes were opened, it says, he saw chariots and four-horse chariots and horses round about (2 Kgs 6:17). In this fiery chariot Elijah too was snatched up to heaven, when Elisha cried: My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer (2 Kgs 2:12). All these things are related, not that God has chariots or four-horse chariots, or is carried by the swiftness of horses, he of whom it is written elsewhere: Who walks upon the wings of the winds (Ps 103 [104]:3); but as he is said to sit on a throne when he assumes the bearing of one who judges, so when he comes to vengeance, to subdue his adversaries, he is shown in the bearing of a victor and one who triumphs. Of the fury of the Lord we have often said that it ought to be taken in the same way as his forgetfulness, and repentance, and sorrow, and the other affections which do not befit the majesty of God.
